draft.title: Changing interpretations
card: What historians think about Pompeii and Herculaneum is not fixed. New excavations and new technology add evidence, and views change as a result.

Example: for a long time the eruption was dated to 24 August AD 79, from a medieval copy of a letter by Pliny the Younger. A charcoal inscription found at Pompeii in 2018 suggests a date later in the year, in October.
Technology also helps. Scans, imaging and DNA analysis can reveal details of buildings and victims without damaging them.
Historians therefore treat their conclusions as the best reading of the evidence so far, and they may revise them.
draft.remember: New finds and methods can overturn old views, so interpretations of the towns can change.

a.q: Why can historians' views of Pompeii change over time?
opts: New evidence and methods can show old views were incomplete
Old sources are thrown out once they are a century old
The towns themselves change shape after each excavation
Historians pick whichever view is most popular
a.why: Fresh finds and better tools can show gaps or errors in earlier views. Old sources are not discarded for age alone, and views are tested against evidence, not popularity.
a.clue: What do new digs and tools give historians?

b.q: A 2018 inscription suggests the eruption came later in the year than the traditional date. What does this best show about the traditional date?
opts: It is open to revision when new evidence appears
It was invented by Pliny the Younger
It has been proved to be correct
It is now useless to historians
b.why: The inscription is new evidence that conflicts with the older date, so the date is open to revision. It does not make the older date useless, because the source it came from still matters, and nothing here shows it was invented.
b.clue: A single new find can challenge an old conclusion.
